original_summary: In Knaresborough on 8 February 1745, Eugene Aram and Richard Houseman murdered the shoemaker Daniel Clarke, who had gathered silver and jewels on credit. Clarke disappeared, and Aram lived and worked as a respectable schoolmaster for fourteen years. In 1758, a skeleton was found near St. Robert's Cave, and Houseman's panic during the inquiry led to his confession and the discovery of a second skeleton in the place he identified. Aram was arrested, tried at York in August 1759, convicted despite his learned defence, and executed on 16 August 1759.
seed_elements: Eugene Aram and Richard Houseman persuade Daniel Clarke to walk out at night to discuss how to dispose of the silver and jewels, then murder him in Knaresborough on 8 February 1745.
Aram remains apparently respectable and untroubled as a schoolmaster in different English towns for fourteen years while Clarke is believed to have disappeared with the goods.
A labourer accidentally uncovers a human skeleton near St. Robert's Cave in 1758, beginning a coroner's inquiry in which Aram's estranged wife expresses her suspicion of Aram and Houseman.

When asked to handle a bone, Houseman panics and says, "This is no more Daniel Clarke's bone than it is mine!" The remark makes people suspicious because they wonder how he could know that unless he had seen Clarke's real bones.

Houseman's confession identifies the true burial place precisely: the head lies a little farther to the right than the first skeleton. People dig there and find a second skeleton exactly where he said.

Aram is arrested at his teaching post, tried at York, gives an eloquent written defence that the bones prove nothing, but is convicted and executed; he privately confesses his guilt to attending clergymen.
discarded_elements: The full historical and legal detail of Aram's written courtroom defence; retain only its basic argument that the bones prove nothing.
Excessive period background about Knaresborough, the cave, and the original investigation that does not move the plot forward.
Graphic or extended detail about Aram's later actions in his cell before execution; end with the execution plainly.
Any invented names, dialogue, motives, or psychological explanations; in particular, do not add details beyond the documented jealousy claim when referring to motive.
conversion_plan: Keep the historical English setting, the real names, dates, and sequence of events, and write in third person with a matter-of-fact, non-sensational tone. Shape it as a 320-380-word A2-level retelling, using short, clear sentences while preserving the murder, fourteen years of apparent respectability, the bone inquiry, Houseman's exact exclamation and precise second burial site, the trial, and the outcome. Compress the long defence and other period detail rather than inventing dialogue or new motives.
